opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be back.

I think the biggest shift is that v1 was quite linear. You started from a human-written code template, the system proposed an idea, made some edits to that template, ran the experiments once, and wrote it up. It was a pipeline, and science doesn't really work like a pipeline. Real research is messy and branching. You try something, it fails, you debug, you go down a side path, you come back.

So in v2 we tried to capture that exploratory, iterative nature more faithfully. The core change is an agentic tree search over experiments. Instead of committing to a single trajectory, the system maintains a tree of experimental nodes. Some are buggy and get debugged, some get refined, and promising ones get expanded further. That's much closer to how a PhD student actually works: you don't just run one experiment, you build up a set of attempts and gradually figure out what's going on.

We also removed the dependence on those hand-crafted templates. In v1 a human had essentially scoped the problem and set up the codebase. In v2 the system works much more open-endedly. It generates ideas, grounds them against the literature, and writes the experimental code more or less from scratch. That's harder, but it means the system is doing more of the actual scientific work rather than filling in blanks.

We also structured the process into stages, a bit like a research project naturally unfolds. First you get a basic working prototype, then you tune hyperparameters, then you run the main agenda of experiments, and finally you do ablations to understand which components actually matter. An experiment manager agent oversees that progression and decides when to move on. Ablations in particular are such an important part of the scientific method, and v1 didn't really treat them as a first-class concern.

Another piece I'm excited about is the feedback loop on figures. We use a vision-language model to critique the plots, checking whether they're readable, whether the captions match what's shown, whether the figure actually supports the claim. Communicating results is part of science too, and that kind of reflection made the papers noticeably better.

The milestone people talked about was that one of the generated papers got through peer review at an ICLR workshop. I want to be careful there. It was a workshop, not the main conference, and we withdrew it afterwards because we'd agreed with the organizers that this was an experiment, and the community hasn't yet settled the norms for AI-generated papers. Interestingly, the paper reported a negative result, something that didn't work as hoped. I actually think that's a nice reflection of the scientific method: honestly reporting what you found, even when it isn't a flashy win.

So I wouldn't say v2 is doing science the way a great human researcher does. There are still plenty of failure modes: hallucinated citations, shallow ideas, overclaiming. But structurally, I think it's a step from "automated paper writing" towards "automated open-ended exploration," and that's the part of the scientific method I care most about.

r002.rationale: It describes research as messy and branching and says promising experimental nodes are expanded, but does not clearly state that human findings guide which experiments to pursue next.

r003.rationale: It discusses failed attempts and negative results but does not connect hypothesis rejection to Karl Popper’s falsificationism.

r004.rationale: It identifies agentic tree search over experiments as v2’s core change and describes maintaining, debugging, refining, and expanding experimental nodes.

r005.rationale: It says v2 removes dependence on hand-crafted templates and is more open-ended, but does not attribute applicability to more settings to that change.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the big difference, I'd say, is that v1 was still quite template-bound. We gave it a starting codebase, a hand-written template for a particular domain, and it would make incremental edits to that template, run experiments, and write the paper. That worked, but it meant a human had already done a lot of the scientific scaffolding: the problem framing, the baseline, the evaluation setup. It was more like a very capable research assistant iterating inside a box we'd drawn.

With v2 we tried to remove that box. There's no template anymore. You hand it a broad research direction, and it has to generate the hypotheses, figure out what the baseline should even be, write the code from scratch, and then decide which results are worth pursuing. The core of it is an agentic tree search over experiments. Instead of a single linear loop, it branches: it proposes several ideas, implements them, runs them in parallel, and then an experiment-manager agent looks at the results and decides which branches to expand and which to prune. That's much closer to how an actual lab works. You don't commit to one path; you try things, most of them fail, and the failures inform what you try next.

The other piece I'd highlight is the staged structure. We explicitly separated the process into phases: get a preliminary version working, then tune hyperparameters, then run the ablations and the broader research agenda. Each stage has its own success criteria, and the system has to pass through them. That mirrors the scientific method in a way v1 didn't, because v1 would sometimes jump straight to writing up something it hadn't really stress-tested.

And then there's the vision-language feedback loop for the write-up. v2 actually looks at the figures it produces, checks whether the plots make sense, whether the captions match, and revises. It sounds mundane, but a lot of science is that kind of self-checking, and it was one of the things reviewers in the v1 era rightly criticized.

I want to be careful not to oversell it, though. The fact that one of the v2 papers got through workshop peer review at ICLR was a meaningful milestone, but we were very upfront that it was a workshop, the acceptance rate was high, and we withdrew the papers. It still makes mistakes a grad student wouldn't make, and it's still quite far from doing the kind of judgment call about what matters that defines good science. What v2 did show is that you can remove the human-written template and the system still produces something coherent end to end. That's the step from "automating parts of the loop" towards "running the loop," and that was the point.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is that v2 makes the process much more iterative. In v1, we had a fairly fixed pipeline: generate an idea, implement it, run experiments, and write a paper. That captures some of the activities of science, but it doesn’t really capture how your next experiment depends on what you learned from the previous one.

With v2, the experiment process is organized as a tree search. The system can explore different directions, inspect results, refine an approach, or go back and pursue another branch. So you have more of this feedback loop between an idea, the evidence you collect, and what you decide to investigate next.

I wouldn’t say that this means we’ve captured the scientific method in its entirety. But it moves us away from treating research as a recipe and toward treating it as an adaptive search process, where failures and unexpected results can influence the trajectory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is that v2 makes the process much more iterative. With v1, we had a fairly prescribed pipeline: come up with an idea, implement it, run experiments, and write a paper. That captures some of what scientists do, but it doesn’t really capture how much the direction changes as you learn from experiments.

In v2, the experiment manager can explore different branches of a research idea. You run something, look at the result, and then decide: should we debug this, change the approach, or investigate a promising observation more deeply? So the experimental results feed back into what you do next.

We also moved away from relying on a human-provided experiment template. That gives the system more responsibility for constructing the research process itself. I wouldn’t say that makes it a complete model of science, but it moves us from executing a predefined workflow toward a more open-ended cycle of proposing, testing, and revising.
